description:
We are a team of student developers participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We aim to combine creativity, technology, and problem-solving to develop an interactive Space Mission Design Game.

Our project ,Orbit Forge, focuses on space mission planning, spacecraft design, resource management, and mission simulation. We want to create an engaging experience that helps participants understand the engineering decisions and challenges involved in real-world space exploration.
summary:
Orbit Forge is an interactive, educational space mission design and simulation game that allows users to experience the process of planning and managing a lunar exploration mission. Users can customize their spacecraft by selecting scientific instruments, essential spacecraft components, launch vehicles, and orbital configurations while considering factors such as mass, power, budget, communication, and mission lifetime.

The platform guides users through six mission stages, from launch and lunar arrival to scientific operations, data transmission, and mission review. At each stage, users make decisions that influence the mission's performance and final outcome. The application generates a mission score and performance report, allowing users to evaluate their choices, save completed missions, and compare different mission configurations.

Orbit Forge aims to make space exploration concepts more engaging and accessible through interactive learning, decision-making, and simplified mission simulations.
details:
How to play

  1. Target: choose Venus, Mars, Vesta or Jupiter. The page shows the transfer time, the departure and capture delta-v, and how much sunlight reaches the target.
  2. Power & Prop: choose chemical or Hall-thruster propulsion, then set the propellant, solar area, battery size and number of nuclear power sources (RTGs). “Auto-size propellant” solves the rocket equation for you.
  3. Comms & Payload: choose the antenna dish, data buffer, science instruments, and optional avionics redundancy and radiation shielding.
  4. Launch & Check: pick a launcher. A live checklist and the sticky bar at the top show mass, delta-v, power, downlink and budget at all times.
  5. Fly: press Launch and watch the mission unfold, with flares, micrometeoroids and avionics faults along the way. “Run 300 flights” estimates your design’s real odds.

The trade-offs are physical. Jupiter gets about 4% of Earth’s sunlight, so you need RTGs and a big dish. Vesta’s capture burn is too large for chemical propulsion to be practical, and the Hall thruster needs 1500 W and a 40% longer trip. The score is 65% science, 20% budget efficiency and 15% reliability.
